==Problem==
There are three jars. Each of three coins is placed in one of the three jars, chosen at random and independently of the placement of the other coins. What is the expected number of coins in a jar with the most coins?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } \frac{4}{3}\qquad\textbf{(B) } \frac{13}{9}\qquad\textbf{(C) } \frac{5}{8}\qquad\textbf{(D) } \frac{17}{9}\qquad\textbf{(E) } 2</imath>

==Solution 1 (Case Work)==
We have three coins and three jars. Each coin is placed independently and randomly into one of the jars. Let <imath>M</imath> be the maximum number of coins in any jar. We want to compute the expected value of <imath>M</imath>.

Step 1: Count total outcomes

Each coin has <imath>3</imath> choices, so the total number of equally likely placements is <imath>3^3 = 27</imath>.

Step 2: Casework on the maximum number of coins

Case 1:  <imath>M = 1</imath>. This occurs when each jar has exactly one coin. There are <imath>3! = 6</imath> assignments of coins to jars. Hence, <imath>\Pr(M=1) = \frac{6}{27} = \frac{2}{9}</imath>.

Case 2:  <imath>M = 3</imath>. This occurs when all three coins fall into the same jar. There are <imath>3</imath> jars to choose from, so <imath>\Pr(M=3) = \frac{3}{27} = \frac{1}{9}</imath>.

Case 3:  <imath>M = 2</imath>. This occurs when one jar has <imath>2</imath> coins, another jar has <imath>1</imath> coin, and the last jar has <imath>0</imath> coins.  
We can choose which jar gets <imath>2</imath> coins in <imath>3</imath> ways, which jar gets <imath>1</imath> coin in <imath>2</imath> ways, and which <imath>2</imath> coins out of the <imath>3</imath> go into the jar with two coins, so we multiply by <imath>\dbinom{3}{2}</imath>, which is just <imath>3</imath> (note we don't have to do this for the earlier cases because for case <imath>2</imath>, all <imath>3</imath> coins go into one jar, and for case <imath>1</imath>, the factorial already accounts for that). Therefore, there are <imath>3^2 \cdot 2 = 18</imath> outcomes. Thus, <imath>\Pr(M=2) = \frac{18}{27} = \frac{2}{3}</imath>.

Step 3: Compute the expected value The expected value of <imath>M</imath> is <imath> \mathbb{E}[M] = 1 \cdot \frac{2}{9} + 2 \cdot \frac{2}{3} + 3 \cdot \frac{1}{9} </imath>.  
Converting everything to ninths, we have <imath> \mathbb{E}[M] = \frac{2}{9} + \frac{12}{9} + \frac{3}{9} = \frac{17}{9} </imath>.

Hence, the expected number of coins in the jar with the most coins is<imath>\boxed{\text{(D) }\frac{17}{9}}</imath>
.

<imath>Pr</imath>=Probability of

<imath>\mathbb{E}</imath>=Expected value

===Another way of finding cases of M = 2===
As described in the solution, there are <imath>3^3=27</imath> ways of distributing the coins into the <imath>3</imath> jars. Because there are <imath>6</imath> ways for M=1 and <imath>3</imath> ways for M=3, there are <imath>27 - 6 - 3 = 18</imath> ways for <imath>M=2</imath>.

==Solution 2 (Fast)==

Assuming all jars and coins are distinct, there are <imath>27</imath> total outcomes. <imath>3!=6</imath> of them distribute exactly, and thus a max of, <imath>1</imath> per cup, <imath>3</imath> ways to choose a jar to put all <imath>3</imath> coins in for a max of <imath>3</imath>. This leaves <imath>27-6-3=18</imath> for a max of <imath>2</imath>, so the expected value is <imath> \frac{6 \cdot 1 + 18 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 3}{27} = \boxed{\text{(D) }\frac{17}{9}}</imath>

==Solution 3 (Circular Counting - Expectation Cycles)==

In circular counting, expected value is determined as
<cmath>
\mathbb{E}_C n(A) = \frac{C n(A)}{\mathbb{T} - C n(A) - n(A)}
</cmath>
Where \( \mathbb{E}_C n(A) \) is the expected value, \( C n(A) \) is the circular gap theorem, \( \mathbb{T} \) is the total number of cases, and \( n(A) \) is the invalid cases.

Arrange the three jars and three coins into a circle of 6 elements. We want to count all the ways in which no 2 or no 3 coins are next to one another. This can easily be done using the circular gap theorem, which states
<cmath>
C n(A) = \frac{n}{k} \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
</cmath>
Where \( n \) is the number of elements in our circle and \( k \) is the number of non adjacencies, in which we wish to count \( n = 6 \) and \( k \in \{1,2,3\} \) (The reason we have only 1, 2, and 3 is because if we have \( n=6 \) and \( k \ge 4 \), we see that the combinatorial part of \( C n(A) \) becomes invalid).

So we begin counting.

For \( k=1 \), using the formula, we have \( \frac{6}{1} \binom{4}{0} \) which is 6.

For \( k=2 \), using the formula, we have \( \frac{6}{2} \binom{3}{1} \), which is 9.

For \( k=3 \), using the formula, we have \( \frac{6}{3} \binom{2}{2} \) which is 2.

Thus we have \( C_6(k \in \{1,2,3\}) = 6+9+2 = 17 \).

Now we calculate the denominator of \( \mathbb{E}_C n(A) \). We see the total number of cases is \( 3^3 = 27 \). So we can find \( \mathbb{T} - C n(A) \). We check for \( n(A) \), in which through common sense, we can see that if the triplet <imath>(a,b,c)</imath> represents the number of coins given to each jar, the triplet <imath>(1,1,1)</imath> doesn't satisfy the condition, as all jars have an equal number of coins. Therefore \( n(A)=1 \).

Our answer is
<cmath>
\mathbb{E}_C n(A) = \frac{C n(A)}{\mathbb{T} - C n(A) - n(A)}
</cmath>
<cmath>
\mathbb{E}_C n(A) = \frac{17}{27-17-1}
</cmath>
<cmath>
\mathbb{E}_C n(A) = \boxed{\text{(D) }\frac{17}{9}}
</cmath>

~Pinotation

==Solution 4 (Weighted Probabilities)==

WLOG label the jars as <imath>1,2,3</imath> and the coins as <imath>a,b,c</imath>. The probability for a given coin to land in a given jar is <cmath>\frac{1}{3}</cmath>The number of ways for all three coins to land in the same jar is <imath>3</imath>, either all in jar <imath>1</imath>, all in jar <imath>2</imath>, or all in jar <imath>3</imath>. Next, the number of ways to have two coins in one jar and one in another in another is <imath>3^2 \cdot 2 = 18</imath>. Finally, since there are <imath>3^3=27</imath> ways, the last weight is <cmath>27-18-3=6</cmath> Thus <cmath>\frac{1}{27} \cdot 3 \cdot 3 + \frac{1}{27} \cdot 2 \cdot 18 + \frac{1}{27} \cdot 1 \cdot 6</cmath>Thus we get <cmath>\boxed{\text{(D) }\frac{17}{9}}</cmath>

~Aeioujyot

==Solution 5==
Denote the expected number of coins in a jar with the most coins as <imath>E</imath>

    Process
    └── The 1st coin must add 1 to <imath>E</imath>. Situation: (1, 0, 0)
        ├── The 2nd coin has <imath>1/3</imath> chance to add 1 to <imath>E</imath>. Situation: (2, 0, 0)
        │   └── The 3rd coin has <imath>1/3</imath> chance to add 1 to <imath>E</imath>. Situation: (3, 0, 0)
        └── The 2nd coin has <imath>2/3</imath> chance to leave <imath>E</imath> unchanged. Situation: (1, 1, 0)
            └── The 3rd coin has <imath>2/3</imath> change to add 1 to <imath>E</imath>. Situation: (2, 1, 0)

Hence, <imath>E = 1 + \dfrac{1}{3} \times (1 + \dfrac{1}{3} \times 1) + \dfrac{2}{3} \times (0 + \dfrac{2}{3} \times 1) = \boxed{\text{(D) }\frac{17}{9}}</imath>

==Solution 6== 
Create a tree diagram and add up the probabilities.

<imath>P = \frac{3}{9} + \frac{2}{9} + \frac{2}{9} + \frac{2}{9} + \frac{2}{9} + \frac{2}{9} + \frac{2}{9} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{9} = \boxed{\text{(D)}\frac{17}{9}}</imath>

Note:
(It does not matter which jar you pick at the head of the diagram so long a you stay consistent)

==Solution 7(Similar to Solution 4)==

We have <imath>3</imath> cases namely

All <imath>3</imath> coins are in exactly one jar.
<imath>2</imath> coins are in one jar and the last one is in one of the other two jars.
Each jar has exactly <imath>1</imath> coin.

For the first case, we note that there are exactly <imath>3</imath> ways all coins are in one of the three jars.
For the second case, we note that we have <imath>3</imath> ways to select the jar that are <imath>2</imath> coins and <imath>2</imath> ways to select the jar that has <imath>1</imath> coin which results in <imath>3 \cdot 2 = 6</imath> ways. However, there are <imath>\binom{3}{2}</imath> ways to select <imath>2</imath> out of the three coins to put in the jar that has <imath>2</imath> coins. This results in <imath>6 \cdot \binom{3}{2} = 18</imath> ways.
Finally, the third case results in <imath>3! = 6</imath> ways since there are <imath>3</imath> ways to select one of the coins to put in jar <imath>1</imath> and <imath>2</imath> ways to select the remaining coins to put in jar <imath>2</imath> and lastly only the last coin can go in jar <imath>3</imath> which results in <imath>1</imath> way. Obviously, this gives <imath>3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 3! = 6</imath> ways.
Finally, we execute the expected value. The probability for each jar is obviously <imath>(\frac{1}{3})^3 = \frac{1}{27}</imath>. Remember to include the value of each expected value as well. Case 1 has a value of <imath>3</imath>, case 2 has a value of <imath>2</imath>, and case 1 has a value of <imath>1</imath> since each of these values is exactly the maximum number of coins in each case. We finally have

<imath>\frac{1}{27} \cdot 3 \cdot 3 + \frac{1}{27} \cdot 18 \cdot 2 + \frac{1}{27} \cdot 6 \cdot 1 = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{4}{3} + \frac{2}{9} = \frac{5}{3} + \frac{2}{9} = \frac{15}{9} + \frac{2}{9} = \frac{17}{9}</imath> so the answer is <imath>D</imath>.

== Solution 8 (Cheese) ==

(Use if you don't know how expected value works).

Since we know that there has to be at least <imath>1</imath> coin in the jar with the most coins, we can instantly rule out answer choice <imath>C</imath>, as <imath>5/8 < 1</imath>. We also know <imath>E</imath> can't be the answer, as there are more cases to get <imath>1</imath> as the most rather than <imath>3</imath>. Since we also know there a majority of cases of <imath>2</imath>, the answer will lean towards <imath>2</imath>, giving us answer choice <imath>D</imath>.
~mugim
